doc.title: Luther Henderson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The Clap Hands records for Columbia
summary: He explains the 1959 Clap Hands albums: cover albums for TV musical directors with standards given a clapping treatment.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: I want to close this part of our session today, ending with your solo career for Columbia Records. Tell me about … and I have to tell you, I've looked and I've looked and it's very difficult to find those records.
'Cause I was gonna bring some to have you sign.
You talkin' about the Clap Hand series and that stuff?
Yes. Tell me what they were, tell me briefly what you were trying to do during that time.
All right, what I was doing at that time, what I was trying to do, first of all, I was
I'm gonna say this is 1959 we're talking about.

Right. I was musical director for Polly Bergen on a regular basis for her regular weekly show, or every two weeks, I believe it was. At any rate, and as such there was Peter Matz, Irv Kostel, various of us who were musical directors for these shows, were called upon by the various records companies to quote unquote cover the hit parade. In other words, we would put out an album of the hits of the day and it would be a gig for us, you know. None of us ever expected to make too much money out of it because … but that was that gig. Now what I hoped to do was to take not hits of the day but some standard things which since I had that particular chance and I was involved in the television in that fashion and give them, give the audience something a little more than just pseudo-jazz to do. I thought what better than to clap hands. And so the first album was called Clap Hands with Luther Henderson. And then Clap Hands with the Westerns and Clap Hands …. see this is what the record company will do... I think they clap hands sold little bit. So then they found that they would have to just keep on doing more and more and more. And guess it finally petered out, you know what I mean? But this is what
I wanted to do and the records, I have them and I'll tell you where I got 'em. I think I paid $50 for one over at (laughs)
in New York at 49th Street. Was that?
